display_name: Terre del Barolo Arnaldo Rivera, Barolo
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Barolo is built for the long game, and Terre del Barolo Arnaldo Rivera sits in the style that makes that point clear: Nebbiolo’s rose-petal lift, firm tannin, and slow-burning savory depth. The 2018, 2016, 2015, 2013, and 2012 medals tell you this is not a trophy-hunter wine; it is a reliable Barolo for people who want the grape’s architecture without paying cru-level money.",
  "wine_summary": "This wine matters because it gives you a straight read on Barolo: 100% Nebbiolo from the Langhe, made under the Barolo rules that require at least 38 months before release, with 18 months in wood. That aging requirement is not bureaucratic trivia; it is why Barolo arrives with tannin that feels built, not raw, and why the wine can shift from red fruit to dried flowers, leather, tar, and truffle as it ages.\n\nTerre del Barolo is a cooperative, which matters in a practical way: you are usually buying breadth and consistency across a range of growers rather than a single-vineyard thesis. Arnaldo Rivera sits in that lane well. The real value here is that it can deliver Barolo’s signature structure and perfume at a price below many estate-bottled bottlings from the famous communes, especially when compared with bottlings from La Morra or Serralunga that often ask for much more money. If you want the shape of Barolo in the glass — not just the name on the label — this is the kind of wine that teaches it.",
  "terroir_expression": "Barolo’s split personality comes from geology. Western communes such as La Morra and Barolo sit on younger Tortonian calcareous marl from the Sant’Agata Fossili formation, which tends to give Nebbiolo more lifted aromatics, softer tannins, and earlier drinkability; eastern communes like Serralunga d’Alba and Monforte rest on older Helvetian sandstone and compact Lequio Formation marl, where the wines turn darker, firmer, and more mineral in feel because the soils are denser and often richer in iron and manganese. In a multi-source Barolo like this, that mix usually translates into red cherry, dried rose, licorice, and a tannic spine that feels dry and persistent rather than plush.\n\nThe climate matters too: the Langhe’s continental pattern brings hot summer days, cool nights, and autumn fog — the nebbiolo-producing fogs are part of the grape’s name and part of its slow ripening. That diurnal swing preserves acidity, so the wine tastes taut and mouthwatering even when the fruit has moved beyond fresh cherry into dried berry and herb territory.",
  "vinification_summary": "Barolo law forces the winemaker to think about time, not just extraction: at least 18 months in oak and 38 months total from November 1 of the harvest year. For Nebbiolo, that oak period helps knit together tannin, color, and aromatic volatility; small barrels can add oxygen faster, while larger botti usually keep the wood footprint quieter, letting tar, rose, and cherry stay central. The key technical point is maceration and aging: long skin contact pulls out Nebbiolo’s famously firm tannins, and the extended maturation softens them enough to drink without destroying the grape’s line.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Pappardelle with braised rabbit ragù — the wine’s acidity cuts the richness, while Nebbiolo’s tannin handles the meat’s gelatin and long-cooked texture.",
    "Nashville hot chicken with collard greens — the spice needs acidity and structure, and Barolo’s dried cherry and savory edge cools the heat without going sweet.",
    "Beef short rib with polenta in a serious trattoria or steakhouse setting — the tannin locks onto the collagen, and the wine’s earthiness echoes the braise.",
    "Mushroom risotto with Parmigiano-Reggiano — the mushroom umami and the wine’s truffle-adjacent notes line up cleanly, and the acid keeps the dish from feeling heavy.",
    "Aged Castelmagno with hazelnut crostini at the end of a fine-dining meal — the salt and fat soften tannin, while the nutty, savory profile meets Nebbiolo where it lives."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Barolo from La Morra — comparable for perfume and red-fruited lift, but often a little softer and more immediately approachable because of the Sant’Agata Fossili marl.",
    "Barbaresco from the central hills around Neive and Treiso — same grape, similar aromatic profile, usually a touch earlier-drinking and slightly less muscular than Barolo.",
    "Langhe Nebbiolo from a serious producer — a lighter, shorter-lived version of the same grape character, useful if you want the Nebbiolo profile without Barolo’s aging and price."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Medium-bodied dry Nebbiolo with firm tannins, high acidity, and rose-and-tar savor",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 2018 now through the next 6-10 years, and 2016, 2015, 2013, and 2012 can go longer if stored at 12-14°C with stable humidity and little vibration. Decant younger bottles for 1-2 hours; older bottles need a gentler pour and less air.",
  "value_assessment": "$35-$60 is the range where this makes sense, and at that level it beats a lot of entry Barolo from Fontanafredda and Marchesi di Barolo on honesty of structure and Nebbiolo character. It is worth it if you want real Barolo without paying for a single cru or a cult bottling; the tradeoff is less site specificity, not less seriousness.",

parsed.hook: Barolo is built for the long game, and Terre del Barolo Arnaldo Rivera sits in the style that makes that point clear: Nebbiolo’s rose-petal lift, firm tannin, and slow-burning savory depth. The 2018, 2016, 2015, 2013, and 2012 medals tell you this is not a trophy-hunter wine; it is a reliable Barolo for people who want the grape’s architecture without paying cru-level money.
parsed.wine_summary:
This wine matters because it gives you a straight read on Barolo: 100% Nebbiolo from the Langhe, made under the Barolo rules that require at least 38 months before release, with 18 months in wood. That aging requirement is not bureaucratic trivia; it is why Barolo arrives with tannin that feels built, not raw, and why the wine can shift from red fruit to dried flowers, leather, tar, and truffle as it ages.

Terre del Barolo is a cooperative, which matters in a practical way: you are usually buying breadth and consistency across a range of growers rather than a single-vineyard thesis. Arnaldo Rivera sits in that lane well. The real value here is that it can deliver Barolo’s signature structure and perfume at a price below many estate-bottled bottlings from the famous communes, especially when compared with bottlings from La Morra or Serralunga that often ask for much more money. If you want the shape of Barolo in the glass — not just the name on the label — this is the kind of wine that teaches it.
parsed.terroir_expression:
Barolo’s split personality comes from geology. Western communes such as La Morra and Barolo sit on younger Tortonian calcareous marl from the Sant’Agata Fossili formation, which tends to give Nebbiolo more lifted aromatics, softer tannins, and earlier drinkability; eastern communes like Serralunga d’Alba and Monforte rest on older Helvetian sandstone and compact Lequio Formation marl, where the wines turn darker, firmer, and more mineral in feel because the soils are denser and often richer in iron and manganese. In a multi-source Barolo like this, that mix usually translates into red cherry, dried rose, licorice, and a tannic spine that feels dry and persistent rather than plush.

The climate matters too: the Langhe’s continental pattern brings hot summer days, cool nights, and autumn fog — the nebbiolo-producing fogs are part of the grape’s name and part of its slow ripening. That diurnal swing preserves acidity, so the wine tastes taut and mouthwatering even when the fruit has moved beyond fresh cherry into dried berry and herb territory.
parsed.vinification_summary: Barolo law forces the winemaker to think about time, not just extraction: at least 18 months in oak and 38 months total from November 1 of the harvest year. For Nebbiolo, that oak period helps knit together tannin, color, and aromatic volatility; small barrels can add oxygen faster, while larger botti usually keep the wood footprint quieter, letting tar, rose, and cherry stay central. The key technical point is maceration and aging: long skin contact pulls out Nebbiolo’s famously firm tannins, and the extended maturation softens them enough to drink without destroying the grape’s line.
food_pairing: Pappardelle with braised rabbit ragù — the wine’s acidity cuts the richness, while Nebbiolo’s tannin handles the meat’s gelatin and long-cooked texture.
Nashville hot chicken with collard greens — the spice needs acidity and structure, and Barolo’s dried cherry and savory edge cools the heat without going sweet.
Beef short rib with polenta in a serious trattoria or steakhouse setting — the tannin locks onto the collagen, and the wine’s earthiness echoes the braise.
Mushroom risotto with Parmigiano-Reggiano — the mushroom umami and the wine’s truffle-adjacent notes line up cleanly, and the acid keeps the dish from feeling heavy.
Aged Castelmagno with hazelnut crostini at the end of a fine-dining meal — the salt and fat soften tannin, while the nutty, savory profile meets Nebbiolo where it lives.
comparable_wines: Barolo from La Morra — comparable for perfume and red-fruited lift, but often a little softer and more immediately approachable because of the Sant’Agata Fossili marl.
Barbaresco from the central hills around Neive and Treiso — same grape, similar aromatic profile, usually a touch earlier-drinking and slightly less muscular than Barolo.
Langhe Nebbiolo from a serious producer — a lighter, shorter-lived version of the same grape character, useful if you want the Nebbiolo profile without Barolo’s aging and price.

parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2018 now through the next 6-10 years, and 2016, 2015, 2013, and 2012 can go longer if stored at 12-14°C with stable humidity and little vibration. Decant younger bottles for 1-2 hours; older bottles need a gentler pour and less air.
parsed.value_assessment: $35-$60 is the range where this makes sense, and at that level it beats a lot of entry Barolo from Fontanafredda and Marchesi di Barolo on honesty of structure and Nebbiolo character. It is worth it if you want real Barolo without paying for a single cru or a cult bottling; the tradeoff is less site specificity, not less seriousness.
parsed.market_position: This lands on restaurant lists as the by-the-glass-upgrade Barolo and on retail shelves as the first bottle I’d point to for someone moving from Langhe Nebbiolo to the appellation proper. Collectors buy it as a dependable house-style reference, while everyday Barolo drinkers buy it because it delivers the category’s tannin-and-perfume profile without a hard luxury markup.
parsed.insider_take: The mistake is treating this like a second-tier label when it is really a smart Barolo for drinking and learning. If you want the name, the grape, and the structure without paying for vineyard fetishism, this is a strong buy; if you want a wine that screams one commune or one cru, skip it and go straight to a single-vineyard bottling.
